 Print AI Representation: Kuala Lumpur built a highway that turns into a flood drain. Image credits: Chatgpt Kuala Lumpur has a tunnel that serves two purposes. During normal weather, drivers use it to travel between the city centre and the southern gateway at Sungai Besi. When heavy rain raises river levels, the same underground structure helps divert excess water away from flood-prone parts of the city. Known as the Stormwater Management and Road Tunnel or SMART Tunnel, the system was completed in May 2007, according to MMC Corporation, one of its builders. The Institution of Civil Engineers describes it as the world’s longest multipurpose tunnel. To accommodate floodwater from the Klang and Ampang Rivers, as well as to alleviate traffic on the road towards Sungai Besi, the Malaysian government created the project known as SMART. This included construction of a 9.7 km dedicated flood conveyance tunnel with a 3 km, double-deck highway. The highway extends from the Kampung Pandan area, through to the Kuala Lumpur-Seremban Expressway at TUDM Airfield in Sungai Besi. According to the Department of Irrigation and Drainage Malaysia, the system was designed to manage excess water from the Klang-Ampang catchment. How the tunnel diverts flood water The floodwater route is adjacent to Kampung Berembang, which is located at the juncture of the Klang and Ampang rivers. When river levels are high, most of the excess water is diverted into a holding pond and then through the bypass tunnel before it reaches the attenuation pond in Taman Desa. From there, the water is discharged into the Kerayong River through a dual box culvert. Four operating modes control traffic and water flow SMART has four operating modes, depending on the levels of rainfall and river conditions. Mode one, which is the normal operating condition, has the motorway fully operational and no diversion of flood water. Mode two begins when flow at the L4 monitoring station is between 70 and 150 cubic metres per second. In this case, water starts to flow through the lower drainage section of the tunnel while traffic continues to use the motorway above. If the flow in the rivers is above 150 cubic metres per second, mode three applies and the motorway is closed and evacuated, which normally takes around an hour. During this time, the water again passes through the lower drainage section of the tunnel, while the motorway decks are kept clear in case mode four is needed. If the storm eases before mode four is needed, the motorway can reopen within 2 to 8 hours of closing, according to the SMART Tunnel’s operational modes. Entrance to Kuala Lumpur's SMART tunnel. Image credits: Wikimedia Commons Mode four is used when a major storm continues and the system needs more capacity. After traffic has been evacuated, the motorway compartments are also used to carry floodwater. Authorities generally confirm this mode one or two hours after mode three begins. Once the water has passed, the tunnel remains closed for dewatering, cleaning and inspection. Reopening can take up to four days from the initial closure. A system designed for a specific flood catchment A real-time flood detection and forecasting system helps authorities monitor rainfall, river flow and water levels. These readings guide decisions about when to change operating modes and whether traffic must leave the tunnel. The Institution of Civil Engineers identifies MMC Corporation Berhad as the project’s structural engineer and Mott MacDonald as the consulting engineer. Join conversation

 The tunnel was built by a joint venture of MMC Corporation Berhad and Gamuda Berhad. Construction lasted about four years and the tunnel opened in 2007. SMART does not eliminate all flood risk in Kuala Lumpur. Its role is limited to water from the Klang-Ampang catchment, so flooding caused by rainfall or reverse flow outside this area cannot be managed through the tunnel. However, it gives the city a way to divert excess water from two major river catchments while keeping an important road connection available during less severe storms.
